source.title: Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory
source.authors: Run-Xi Cheng; Yu-Chen Guan; Yong-Xian Wei; Qian-Pu Sun; Qi-Xiu Li; Si-Nan Du; Feng Xiong; Chun Yuan; Yan Lu; Yeyun Gong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figures are flattened into the text, and exact plotted loss values are not provided.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the original scaling-law work as background and for compute accounting, but does not test the stated parameter/token/compute power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its memory-capacity loss sweep is a related but different scaling result.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a training-loss trend as grafted external-memory capacity increases. This is recorded under fits_no_version: it varies memory-bank entries, not parameter count, training tokens, or compute, and it reports training loss rather than held-out pretraining loss. The benchmark comparisons and other training-loss comparisons concern Memory Grafting versus alternative architectures, not the claim's scaling-law behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as background and for compute accounting (Appendix C.1). It proposes an architecture (Memory Grafting) and compares it to MoE and Engram at two fixed scales (0.92B/50B tokens, 2.8B/100B tokens). It fits no power law in parameters, tokens or compute and makes no extrapolation or allocation analysis. The only scaling sweep varies frozen external memory entries (30k, 300k, 3M) and reports training loss curves, with no functional fit. That is a related but different axis.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Memory Grafting improves over MoE and vanilla Engram under matched trainable parameters and token budgets. Gains depend on the grafting model's representation quality and on the source layer. Larger grafted memory lowers training loss, and runtime overhead is modest (0.92x training throughput, 0.95x inference throughput). They present it as a step toward scaling beyond trainable parameters.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and evaluates conditional-memory grafting; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurement or fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported Memory Grafting outcomes vary with grafting-model choice, grafting-model source layer, and memory capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Training loss decreases monotonically as the frozen grafted n-gram memory grows from 30k to 300k to 3M entries. The authors give no power-law fit and no numbers. N-gram hit rate rises with memory size but with diminishing growth (Fig 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In external frozen n-gram memory, recipient training loss falls as memory-bank size grows, with diminishing coverage gains.

record.problems: The memory-capacity loss results are shown as curves without exact numerical values or uncertainty estimates, and they report training loss rather than held-out loss. The experiments do not test the parameter/token/compute scaling laws or extrapolation claims.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; the relevant memory-capacity sweep is represented by rows r1–r3. Other architecture and benchmark comparisons do not measure the claim's scaling-law behavior.

untested.parts: All: no loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute; only two fixed recipient scales are compared across architectures.
All: no fit on small runs used to predict larger ones.
All: there are architecture comparisons (MoE vs Engram vs grafting), but no depth/width sweep at a fixed parameter count.
All: text pretraining only, with no power-law form fitted in another regime.
All: benchmark scores are given at two scales, but across different architectures, with no analysis of predictability with scale or loss.
All: no fitted exponents or comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/cites_only call is correct. The Kaplan and Hoffmann citations appear only in the introduction and in the 6N/2N compute accounting in Appendix C.1. The benchmark tables compare the authors' method against baselines, so they are not claim rows.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute; several orders of magnitude; bottleneck conditions.
Fitting laws on small runs and predicting much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices; departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Memory Grafting
rows.operation_detail: Varied the grafted n-gram memory capacity and measured training loss.
rows.note: The authors state that larger memory capacity gives lower loss throughout training; this is not a numerical power-law fit.
rows.check: This is the smallest point of a memory-capacity sweep and has no comparison of its own. The 'observed' state has no referent: the curve is figure-only and the row is only meaningful relative to r2 and r3. It measures training loss against external memory entries, not against parameters, tokens or compute.

rows.operation_detail: Varied the grafted n-gram memory capacity and measured training loss.
rows.note: The authors state that increasing capacity from 30k to 300k improves the loss curve; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Lower training loss than 30k entries, per the authors' text (Sec 4.3.4). No values are given and no power-law fit is made. Memory entries are not a V1 axis.
